Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is generally understood as a set of methods and techniques designed to make the behaviour and outputs of AI systems understandable to humans. This field bridges the gap between high-performing but opaque models—such as deep neural networks—and the need for interpretability, enabling stakeholders like users, developers, and regulators to grasp why an AI system arrived at a particular decision. XAI is often described as essential for fostering trust in AI, particularly in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, finance, and criminal justice, where accountability and transparency are critical. Common approaches include model-agnostic methods like LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) and SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations), as well as inherently interpretable models such as decision trees or linear models with transparent feature contributions. The distinction between interpretability and explainability is central to XAI. Interpretability refers to the intrinsic transparency of a model—how easily its internal logic can be understood—while explainability pertains to the ability to provide post-hoc explanations for a model’s outputs, even when the model itself is not inherently interpretable. For example, saliency maps can highlight which parts of an image influenced a neural network’s classification, offering explanations without altering the underlying model. This duality reflects broader debates in AI ethics about balancing performance with human-centred design, where trade-offs between accuracy and transparency often arise.
